s: A. The Youngstown framework.
In 1952, facing a nationwide steel strike during the Korean War, President Truman ordered the Secretary of Commerce to seize and operate the steel mills.
In Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, the Court held the seizure unconstitutional.
Justice Black's majority opinion was formalist: the order was lawmaking, which belongs to Congress.
Justice Jackson's concurrence became the governing framework.
Jackson's three categories (Youngstown concurrence).
Maximum authority.
The President acts pursuant to express or implied authorization of Congress.
His power includes all he possesses in his own right plus all Congress can delegate.
The action is invalid only if the federal government as a whole lacks the power.
Zone of twilight.
Congress has neither granted nor denied authority.
The President relies on his independent powers, and the outcome depends on "the imperatives of events and contemporary imponderables," including congressional inertia and historical practice.
Lowest ebb.
The President acts against the express or implied will of Congress.
He can rely only on his own constitutional powers minus Congress's powers over the matter, and courts sustain such action only if the power is "conclusive and preclusive."
The framework recurs across modern disputes.
Dames & Moore v. Regan (1981) found implied congressional acquiescence in claims settlements with Iran (category one or two).
Medellín v. Texas (2008) placed the President's memorandum ordering state courts to comply with an ICJ judgment in category three and struck it down.
Zivotofsky v. Kerry (2015) held the recognition power exclusive to the President, so it prevailed even at the lowest ebb.
Trump v. Hawaii (2018) upheld a proclamation restricting entry under broad statutory delegation (category one).
